 1           II.       ASSIGNMENT AND SUMMARY OF TESTIMONY AND
 2                            RECOMMENDATIONS

 3   Q.   What is the purpose of your testimony?

 4   A.   My testimony describes the Transmission business area and supports SPS’s request to

5         recover transmission capital additions and Operation and Maintenance (“O&M”)

6         expense through its base rates. I explain why these investments are reasonable,

7         necessary, and beneficial to SPS’s New Mexico retail customers, even when the

8         underlying projects are located in Texas or Oklahoma or serve multiple states within

 9        the Southwest Power Pool.       SPS operates one integrated transmission system.

10        Strengthening that system improves reliability, increases transfer capability, supports

11        renewable generation deliveries, and reduces congestion costs for New Mexico

12        customers.

13   Q.   What are the Base Period, Linkage Data Timeframe, and Future Test Year

14        Period?

15   A.   The Base Period is July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025. The Linkage Data

16        Timeframe runs from the end of the Base Period to the beginning of the Future Test

17        Year, from July 1, 2025 through November 30, 2026. The Future Test Year Period

18        covers December 1, 2026, through November 30, 2027. These periods are used

                                              of
                                       Reene Miranda

 1        throughout my testimony to present SPS’s transmission capital additions and O&M

 2        adjustments.

 3   Q.   How does SPS use the Linkage Data in this case?

 4   A.   For capital additions, the Linkage Data captures transmission projects that SPS

 5        expects to place in service after the Base Period and before the Future Test Year

 6        Period. Those projects are listed in Table RM-1. For O&M, the Linkage Data does

7         not represent a separate forecast. It shows the discrete, known, and measurable

8         adjustments applied to the Adjusted Base Period amounts to create a verifiable link

9         to the Future Test Year Period. This approach is consistent with Rule 17.1.3.7(H)

10        NMAC, which provides that linkage data does not constitute a test period but is

11        presented to validate the Future Test Year Period information.

12   Q.   What specific subjects does your testimony cover?

13   A.   My testimony addresses three topics:        First, I explain how SPS identifies,

14        prioritizes, and manages new capital projects within the transmission business area

15        and describe the controls that ensure those projects are completed cost-effectively.

16        Second, I present and support the transmission capital additions that have been or

17        will be placed in service during the Base Period, the Linkage Data Timeframe, and

18        the Future Test Year Period, and I explain why these additions are prudent,

 1        III.       THE RANKING, ESTIMATION, AND MANAGEMENT OF
 2                         TRANSMISSION CAPITAL ADDITIONS

 3   Q.    Please describe the Transmission business area and the work that the

 4         Transmission business area performs to support SPS’s operations.

 5   A.    The Transmission business area supports reliable, cost-effective, and timely

 6         engineering solutions for constructing, operating, and maintaining high-voltage

 7         transmission lines and substations to support system reliability and to strengthen

 8         the infrastructure necessary to serve SPS’s customers. SPS uses that infrastructure

 9         to transmit electricity from generation facilities to the distribution system, from

10         which SPS delivers power directly to the homes and business of customers.

11   Q.    Please describe the processes for identifying and ranking Transmission capital

12         projects.

13   A.    The Transmission Planning functional area develops and plans transmission

14         projects through technical studies that consider, among other things:

15               •   the need for new distribution load-serving substations;

16               •   the need for transmission upgrades based on the North American Electric
17                   Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) reliability standards;

18               •   new generation and transmission service requests; and

19               •   coordination and planning discussions with the Southwest Power Pool
20                   planning staff.


                                                  9
                                          Case No. 25-00___-UT

                                                   of
                                            Reene Miranda

 1   Q.     Does SPS rely on any third-party recommendations regarding transmission

 2          planning and expansion?

 3   A.     Yes. As part of the Southwest Power Pool’s regional planning process, the

 4          Southwest Power Pool periodically issues to SPS a Notification to Construct

 5          (“NTC”) for the following types of transmission projects: 2

 6          •        projects needed for reliability purposes;

 7          •        projects necessary to provide transmission service under the Southwest
 8                   Power Pool Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”);

 9          •        projects that have been determined by the Southwest Power Pool to provide
10                   regional economic benefits; and

11          •        projects required to provide service to new delivery points under the
12                   Southwest Power Pool OATT.

13   Q.     How does the Southwest Power Pool evaluate transmission needs before

14          issuing an NTC?

15   A.     As SPS witness Jarred J. Cooley explains in his direct testimony, the Southwest

16          Power Pool conducts a rigorous, multi-step review before issuing an NTC. It

17          performs detailed power-flow, stability, contingency, and economic analyses



              2

      by the SPP Board of Directors (Board) intended to meet the construction needs of the SPP

      Transmission Organization (RTO).

 1        across the entire region and vets those results through stakeholder working groups,

 2        technical committees, and its independent Board of Directors. SPS participates in

 3        those processes by providing modeling data, reviewing study assumptions,

 4        evaluating proposed solutions, and commenting on draft recommendations. In

 5        short, the Southwest Power Pool issues an NTC only after it determines that a

 6        project is needed and cost-effective for the region.

 7   Q.   Does SPS provide input or challenge NTCs when appropriate?

 8   A.   Yes. SPS reviews each NTC and may request reevaluation if updated system

 9        information shows that a project may no longer be needed or may require

10        modification. For instance, as Mr. Cooley notes, SPS asked the Southwest Power

11        Pool to revisit an NTC for a 115 kilovolt (“kV”) rebuild between Hereford and

12        Clovis after generation patterns changed. The Southwest Power Pool agreed with

13        SPS’s assessment and cancelled portions of the NTC, avoiding approximately

14        $11.7 million in capital expenditures. This ongoing evaluation demonstrates both

15        SPS’s diligence and the robustness of the Southwest Power Pool’s planning

16        process.

 1   Q.   How does SPS prioritize transmission capital projects?

 2   A.   Key drivers for the risk prioritization strategy include compliance requirements,

 3        contractual agreements, reliability and regulatory mandates, economic benefits,

 4        external requests, and other risk factors.

 5   Q.   What are non-discretionary projects?

 6   A.   Non-discretionary projects are those SPS is legally, contractually, or operationally

 7        obligated to pursue. These projects include the following:

 8           •   work needed to restore power after outages;

 9           •   work that must be performed in accordance with contractual agreements;

10           •   projects that are mandated by regulators;

11           •   projects that have received an NTC;

12           •   projects necessary to connect loads and generators; and

13           •   projects that have received a high ranking during the prioritization process.

14   Q.   Please describe how the Transmission business area develops cost estimates

15        for the funding of proposed Transmission capital additions.

16   A.   Attachment RM-8 outlines the general estimating steps and shows what project

17        information is available as a project goes from concept to construction. When a

18        project is prepared for the capital budget, a preliminary scope is developed by

19        Transmission Planning or other submitting organization and is provided to the

                                                12
                                             Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                              Direct Testimony
                                                      of
                                               Reene Miranda

 1           Project Management organization.                 Project Management then requests cost

 2           estimates from the Substation/Transmission Engineering & Design organization. 3

 3                    If the project is an internally-developed budget item, the initial estimate is

 4           a scoping estimate that is intended to be within ±30% of the total expected project

 5           cost. If the initial estimate is for a generator facilities study or a project proposed

 6           in response to an NTC, the Southwest Power Pool’s tariff includes additional cost

 7           estimation and oversight requirements.

 8   Q.      Does SPS have any additional cost management safeguards as part of the

 9           project planning process?

10   A.      Yes. After the initial cost estimate is developed, each project proceeds through a

11           series of design reviews, called the “Project Lifecycle”. These reviews evaluate the

12           project’s scope, cost, schedule, and feasibility at different stages of development.

13                    The Preliminary Scope Intake review evaluates the validity of the initial

14           scope and identifies any fatal flaws in the proposed project. Once approved, SPS

15           develops a ±30% scoping estimate. The project then advances to a Constructability

16           Review and Site Visit, which includes a field inspection to identify issues not

 1        evident from drawings. If changes are necessary due to issues discovered during a

 2        field visit, the scope is modified. If field conditions require changes, SPS revises

 3        the project scope accordingly.

 4               Next, SPS conducts the “Final Scope Review,” where it develops an

5         appropriation estimate, accurate within ±20 percent, that supports management

6         approval of project funding. After completing final design, but before construction

7         begins, SPS prepares a ±10 percent engineering estimate, the most accurate

 8        estimate prepared for the project. This estimate reflects detailed site information,

 9        actual material costs, and, when available, construction bid pricing. It serves as the

10        final control point for cost and schedule. At this stage, SPS has more detailed

11        information about site conditions and project scope, although external factors such

12        as material delivery, outage timing, or contractor availability may still vary.

13   Q.   Does SPS seek input from other stakeholders during any part of the planning

14        process?

15   A.   Yes. During the “Project Lifecycle”, the planning team coordinates with internal

16        stakeholders from across the company. These stakeholders include representatives

17        from engineering, operations, construction, siting and land rights, regulatory, and



                                               14

 1        other areas with relevant expertise. Stakeholder participation in the process often

 2        depends on the scope and complexity of the project.

 3   Q.   What types of tools does SPS use to assist it in the planning and cost estimate

 4        processes?

 5   A.   SPS uses an estimating software program called InEight Estimate to generate cost

 6        estimates. InEight Estimate contains a database of historical engineering, material,

 7        and construction costs that engineers can draw upon to prepare accurate cost

 8        estimates. Engineers use templates from similar projects to ensure their estimates

 9        include all the necessary cost elements. Any engineering consultants hired to

10        provide estimates use the same process to ensure that their estimates are consistent

11        with the methods used to prepare estimates generated internally.

12   Q.   Please provide an example of how cost estimates were prepared for a

13        representative transmission project.

15        Hereford substation, continuing to the Deaf Smith #6 Tap then to the Friona

16        substation and terminating at the Cargill substation. This project was identified as

17        part of the Southwest Power Pool’s 2020 Integrated Transmission Planning (“ITP”)

 1   Assessment, in which the Southwest Power Pool studied and analyzed local and

 2   regional reliability issues.

 3           The regional reliability upgrade of the T58 transmission circuit was

 4   identified as a needed reliability upgrade in the SPS area driven by thermal

 5   reliability needs, where the T58 circuit overloaded during bus outages of the Deaf

 6   Smith Interchange 115kV bus and Roosevelt 230kV bus.              Although several

 7   substations on this circuit are located in Texas, the circuit is part of the same

 8   integrated transmission network that serves SPS’s New Mexico retail customers.

 9   Improving the thermal performance and contingency resilience of this line

10   enhances the overall stability of the SPS system, supports power flows into eastern

11   New Mexico, and reduces the risk of congestion or service disruptions affecting

12   New Mexico customers.

13           The Southwest Power Pool issued NTC-2010574 along with a conceptual

14   cost estimate, and SPS as part of accepting the NTC provided a refined cost

15   estimate, as required by Southwest Power Pool’s procedures. Within SPS, the

16   project moved through the project management and estimating processes described

17   above. Thus, cost estimates for the project were subject to multiple levels of review

18   and oversight as the project was being developed.

 1   Q.   How does SPS manage transmission capital costs for its projects?

 2   A.   SPS manages transmission capital costs through a structured review and approval

 3        process.   Each project passes budget, management, senior-management, and

 4        executive reviews before SPS authorizes funding. After approval, SPS tracks every

 5        project monthly, comparing forecasted to actual spending and year-to-date results

 6        to interim and year-end forecasts. When variances arise, SPS identifies the cause,

 7        reviews proposed corrections, and approves the actions needed to meet financial

8         targets. The Financial Performance and Planning (“FP&P”) group monitors these

9         reviews and reports on overall capital spending.

10   Q.   How does SPS manage costs for projects directed by the Southwest Power

11        Pool?

12   A.   For each Southwest Power Pool NTC project, SPS reports the estimated completion

13        cost to the Southwest Power Pool every quarter. When a project’s estimated cost

14        exceeds the Southwest Power Pool’s variance thresholds, the Southwest Power

15        Pool Project Cost Working Group and other stakeholder committees review the

16        estimate. If costs fall significantly outside the allowable range, the Southwest

17        Power Pool may accept the variance, modify the project scope to reduce cost,

18        suspend the project for further study, or cancel it.

1    Q.   Does SPS have a process to address contingencies that may arise during a

2         budget period?

3    A.   Yes. SPS’s approved transmission capital budget includes unallocated funds for

4         projects not yet executed when the budget was developed. These funds cover

5         transmission,   generation,   and   transmission-to-transmission   interconnection

6         projects that must move quickly once agreements are finalized.

7    Q.   Why does SPS maintain unallocated funding for interconnection projects?

8    A.   SPS must construct interconnection projects within identified time frames under

 9        the Southwest Power Pool Open Access Transmission Tariff. Unallocated funding

10        lets SPS begin those projects promptly and remain in compliance with those

11        requirements. SPS maintains unallocated transmission dollars in the five-year

12        budget in anticipation of interconnection projects that complete an interconnection

13        agreement, allowing SPS to move forward with engineering and equipment

14        procurement for long lead time material.

15   Q.   How does SPS fund projects that arise outside the original budget cycle?

16   A.   SPS uses available unallocated funds for projects identified after the budget is

17        finalized. When additional funding is needed, SPS seeks approval through the same

18        process used for new capital-budget items, including engineering, management,



                                              18
                                     Case No. 25-00___-UT
                                      Direct Testimony
                                              of
                                       Reene Miranda

 1        and financial review. SPS has a monthly Base Capital meeting to approve dollars

 2        for projects that require initiation outside of the normal yearly budget cycle.

 3   Q.   Does the capital budget include funds for unexpected events?

 4   A.   Yes. SPS budgets for unforeseen events that require capital spending, such as

 5        emergency outages. It bases these amounts on historical costs for repairing failed

 6        or storm-damaged equipment.

 7   Q.   Are the budgeting and project-management processes for projects in the

 8        Linkage Data Timeframe and Future Test Year the same as those used for the

 9        Base Period?

10   A.   Yes. The transmission business area routinely manages multi-year projects and

11        prepares a five-year capital budget each year. That experience allows SPS to

12        develop accurate budgets for known and anticipated work.
